answer.rationale: The release two hours ago is the only new variable that plausibly explains a 90-minute write-path degradation, and memory_b1 records a rollback cleanly resolving a comparable checkout error spike. I want the archived source for memory_b1 to check whether that success was on a write-heavy path or merely a stateless read path, and whether the prior build was schema-compatible /migbackfill was involved / because rolling back across a migration is exactly how you lose customer writes at settlement peak, which is the primary objective's hard constraint. I want memory_b6 because it cuts against my own hypothesis: if canary gating reliably catches regressions within an hour, this build passed that gate, which weakens the release-causation story and would point toward organic load. That is the memory most likely to falsify me, so it is worth the budget. Regional failover is ruled out on memory_b2's explicit and costly lesson / writes are hot right now, and that memory records actual lost writes, which is a direct violation of the objective, not a tradeoff. Capacity addition and read-replica routing (memory_b5) address read-side pressure on the primary and may help, but they are slower and do not address a suspected code-level regression; they remain the fallback if verification undermines the release hypothesis. I am choosing a small guarded scale deliberately: roll back a limited cohort first to confirm causality and confirm no write divergence before any broad action. If the archived records show migration or schema coupling, I will abandon rollback entirely rather than trade availability for data loss. Note the inherited memories are consolidated summaries whose causal claims may be post-hoc; the 30-minute gap between deploy and symptom onset is unexplained and I am not treating release causation as settled.
